request.job_description: We are hiring a Frontend Engineer to build accessible, high-quality product UI in React and TypeScript. You will own features end to end, collaborate with design and backend engineers, ensure components meet WCAG 2.1 AA, write maintainable typed code, and help improve performance and testing practices across the web app.

transcript.question: Tell me about a complex React feature you built recently and how you used TypeScript to keep it maintainable.
transcript.answer: I built a multi-step billing settings flow with about a dozen form states. I modeled the steps as a discriminated union so each step carried only its own data, and a reducer handled transitions with exhaustive switch checks, so adding a step caused compile errors anywhere we forgot to handle it. I also wrote generic typed form field components with inferred value types, which removed a class of bugs where we passed strings to numeric inputs. I'd say it cut form-related bug tickets noticeably, though I didn't track the exact number.

transcript.question: How do you make a custom component, like a dropdown or modal, accessible?
transcript.answer: For a modal I start with the dialog role, aria-modal, and a label tied to the title. Focus has to move into the modal on open, be trapped inside while open, and return to the trigger on close. Escape should close it. For a custom dropdown I follow the ARIA combobox or listbox pattern with arrow key navigation and aria-activedescendant. I test with VoiceOver and NVDA, and I run axe in CI, but I know automated tools only catch roughly a third of issues so I do manual keyboard passes too. Once I found our select was announcing options twice in NVDA because of duplicated aria-labels and fixed it.

transcript.question: Describe a time you improved the performance of a React app.
transcript.answer: Yeah, we had a slow page once and I looked into it. I think I added some memoization and it got faster. It was a list page I believe. We used React.memo in a few places.

transcript.question: How do you approach testing front-end code?
transcript.answer: I write unit tests with React Testing Library and Jest, querying by role and label so tests double as an accessibility check. I avoid testing implementation details like internal state. For critical flows like checkout I add a few Playwright end-to-end tests. I'm less experienced with visual regression testing, we didn't have that setup. On the billing project I think we had around 80 percent coverage on the components, but I focused more on testing behavior than hitting a number.

transcript.question: Tell me about a disagreement with a designer or backend engineer and how you handled it.
transcript.answer: There was a design with a color palette where the secondary button text failed contrast, around 3 to 1. I raised it with the designer, showed the contrast checker result, and proposed a slightly darker shade that kept the brand feel. They agreed after seeing it, and we added contrast tokens to the design system so it wouldn't recur. With backend, I usually just message them when an API shape is awkward and we sort it out.
